title: How to spot plugin s made with A.I

posts.author: Eliaquim
posts.body:
Introduction:
Spoiler
If you don’t mind using plugins made with A.I., you can ignore this post. I'm not trying to convince someone to not use A.I. This is for people who already are convinced that they do not want/like A.I.
This topic has been on my mind for some time. How can a person that does not know how to code, know whether the plugin they are using or buying was made with A.I. or not?
I’ve noticed that many people are against the use of A.I., not only because of the poor quality of what is often produced, but also for moral reasons. And I’ve been noticing a significant number of plugins being sold without stating that they were made with A.I.
This post will not provide a definitive answer. However, my intention is to offer some points that, in my opinion, may help you identify the use of A.I.
And hopefully, others can contribute relevant information to help detect the use of A.I. in plugins.
Context:
Spoiler
Recent events motivated me to write this:
A)
Only on January, I got 3 commissions that was needed from me to take a look at A.I 100% generated codes. On these 3 cases, from different clients, they have buyed the plugins without knowing they are A.I. Two of them, also ended up asking commision me to write a plugin that does what these A.I does. And the other one just gave up for the commission, because I said that I don't look into A.I generated plugins.
B -
I found this in the analytics of one of my plugin pages on itch.io:
C)
Someone made a minimap plugin and posted about it in the thread of my minimap plugin here on the forum, presenting what appeared to be a feature that my plugin does not have. An aggressive marketing strategy, which doesn’t bother me, but it made me curious.
So I checked this person’s post. Among many other pieces of evidence, I found the following:
Analyzing how everything was written, it felt very A.I.-generated to me. That made me think that my plugin’s code was probably placed into a chat for analysis and comparison. And since we’re already here, why not suspect that part of the code may also have been copied or used as learning material to construct another one?(which honestly, I don't bother. I would even teach someone if htey asked me too)
However, this part convinced me that A.I. was definitely used in some way during the process:
“similar to your approach” - Like someone else was talking to the author of the post. Very explicit.
D)
The forum had an access issue a few weeks ago. In my understanding, that also seemed to involve A.I. at some level. At least according to this post by Archeia:
E)
Another reason for creating this thread was another one I saw here related to A.I., but about art. A person (a client) was paying another person (“artist”) to create art for their project. In this case, the artist was using A.I. and did not inform the client. I noticed that many people were against this, as I am as well. That was also one of the things that triggered a “click” for me to write about this, but on the coding side. (if anyone remember the thread, let me know so I can put a link here)
Attention:
Spoiler
Before we move on to some tips on how to notice that a plugin was made with A.I., let me clarify a few things:
1 - I mentioned the points above to provide context for what I am about to say.
2 - Personally, I don’t mind if other people use A.I. to create their plugins. But it seems that, that kind of stuff is already getting into my reality(like I said about doing commissions compatible with A.I plugins). I don’t think it’s honest to sell them without informing that they were made with A.I. When publishing a plugin on itch.io, the author should inform whether A.I. was used or not:
This is different from tags. I don’t know how itch.io signals this to consumers when someone marks that A.I. was used, but it’s something to consider if anyone knows how can spot this...
Now, if there is a warning, then it’s up to the consumer to decide whether to buy it or not.
3 - Another issue with A.I.-generated code, in the RPG Maker context, is when people come to the forum asking for support with code made 100% by A.I., and they have absolutely no idea what is inside it.
Now, let’s get to the point!
Points That Can Be Observed
To notice that someone is selling a plugin made with A.I., you don’t necessarily need to look only at the plugin’s code. You can also observe other parts of the process. Here are some tips that may help you identify a likely A.I.-made plugin. Keep in mind that this is a matter of probability. It will be very rare (I believe) for someone to sell a 100% A.I.-generated code without any modification, to the point where its use is completely obvious.
1 - Icons and emojis
If you notice the use of many icons/emojis in page descriptions and especially in the plugin’s help file, that can already be an indication that A.I. may have been used. These systems often write using such elements. I’ve made compatibility patches and read many plugin codes, and I’ve never seen any using icons or emojis in the help file. Until now haha ^^''
2 - Excessive code comments
In some cases, along with emojis/icons, the plugin’s code itself may contain an excessive amount of obvious comments explaining what a function or piece of code is doing. While comments can be normal depending on the coder, using icons and emojis in them? Strong indication of A.I.
3 - Overly sophisticated language, out of context, or trying to over-explain obvious things
I admit this can be controversial because it’s subjective. There may be cases where people genuinely write this way, or use translators for English. But I think it’s still something to observe.
This is better shown than explained. For example, let’s look at the text below, which I took from the thread mentioned in point C above:
“While the market offers several minimap solutions, this plugin was specifically engineered to solve the problems that often plague development: unreliable architecture, convoluted configuration, and unpredictable behavior that breaks during critical project phases. This isn't just another display tool; it's a production-ready system designed to integrate reliably into your commercial or ambitious hobby project.”
“While the market offers several minimap solutions,” “engineered,” “often plague development,” “unreliable architecture” — do you see it?
“Seamlessly.” “Immersive experience.”
Especially if these kinds of words are being used repeatedly in the same help file or page description.
4 - Plugin bugs/errors
Another tip is when you point out a problem in the plugin to the developer. Notice whether they can actually explain why that issue is happening, or if they usually just say whether they fixed it or not. Sometimes they may even detail the fix in their update log. Of course, they could also use A.I. to explain it…
5 - Whole process
Lastly, also subjective but with strong impact. If the person uses A.I. in multiple parts of the process such as: plugin cover art, YouTube video (voice or thumbnail), page description, or help file — why wouldn’t they also use A.I. in the code?
Well, these are my insights after observing several plugin authors on itch.io, including, but not only, the one I had tried to make a compatibility patch. I won’t name them for ethical reasons, except for the one mentioned in item C, since that person mentioned me too.
Feel free to give suggestions or correct me.
Tips by Att Turan:
Use of Lists
People do not typically write plugin documentation as any kind of list, but the use of lists (bulleted or numbered) by generative AI is
very
prevalent. I've seen a number of plugins that gave instructions on how to use it via a list of numbered steps, and I would immediately suspect that to be AI.
Conversational Comments
For those who aren't familiar with JavaScript, you can open up the plugin in a text editor and search for // to find lines that are comments. In addition to the over-commenting you mentioned (having functions where every line is unnecessarily documented), I have seen plugins where the comments are clearly addressed to the person using the AI.
For example, something like
JavaScript:
// This fixes your pixel shifting issue

posts.author: SGHarlekin
posts.body:
Good post, and I have personally also immediately adapted to just not touch anything that has an AI thumbnail. Not even gonna look at the page. The other pointers are also solid.
One thing I also personally look out for in terms of itch specifically is when their account is new and they release a whole bunch of plugins at once. Of course they
could
technically just made a catalogue beforehand and then released them all at once, but I find that most of the time, this is also combined with all the other points you brought up, so I think it's worth mentioning.
Another small thing to note is that sometimes these "plugin authors" legit forget to remove the "author: chatpgt" line from their file lol.
(Side note: It's a good post, but aren't we just telling the shills what to do to better hide their scams?
)

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
SGHarlekin said:
when their account is new and they release a whole bunch of plugins at once.
Click to expand...
Actually, this is a good rule of thumb for AI generated anything.
Take artists and musicians; typically they have a past portfolio that's spread out over a long time. If suddenly some no name is dropping 3 albums of "Lofi beats to game dev to" that doesn't make sense.
In addition to that, you should be able to see improvements in quality over the span of their portfolio. If some no name suddenly drops a professionally polished beat with no history and no studio behind it, something is sus. Same goes for art too, of course.
Unfortunately this doesn't really transfer to code. Maybe skilled programmers can discern amateur code from professional, but to the general public this isn't much of a short hand to identify AI code.

posts.author: SGHarlekin
posts.body:
Well, on the bright side I think this gives more credibility to the tried and true coders that have been working with us poor little RM devs for decades. Sadly this also means they're overworked and finding legit newer talents to hire is incredibly hard.
Personally I found it to be very effective to skip anything with an AI thumbnail. (I know I'm repeating myself here.)
While you may or may not miss someone legit. (Although chances are low, especially for plugins. A screenshot of your plugin parameters are way more appealing than some squeezed generic hero character holding up a sword.)
Reason I say this again is because this way of dealing with it will save you a lot of time trying to comb through all the other pointers to really try and find out whether or not you found the one guy who legit types 500 emojis in their comments. Save yourselves the trouble and just skip it.

posts.author: Solar_Flare
posts.body:
TheAM-Dol said:
If suddenly some no name is dropping 3 albums of "Lofi beats to game dev to" that doesn't make sense.
Click to expand...
While this is definitely a red flag, I wouldn't 100% dismiss it just from that. It's not just
possible
that someone might've built up a profile in private and suddenly decided to release it; I believe it's entirely plausible that someone would do that, and someone who did that would probably pick their best works to actually release. Still, it should be possible to distinguish those (relatively rare) individuals from people who actually use AI.
If it's plugins, for example, you could probably infer it from their other reactions on the forum. If they're helping people with coding problems in addition to just posting their plugin library, then that library is more likely to be legit.
I'm less sure how that would translate to people posting art or music or even writing. But, I bet you could find some similar sorts of parallels.
ATT_Turan said:
People do not typically write plugin documentation as any kind of list,
Click to expand...
Actually, I do use lists in my plugin documentation and/or itch pages, though not extensively. Currently, all of my plugins currently released on itch have lists in the plugin page; I think only one of them has lists in the actual plugin documentation. I don't remember if any of the plugins not yet on itch use lists. All of the plugins on itch also have a numbered list in the "install instructions" section. I've never used a numbered list anywhere else as far as I can recall.
I can definitely agree that lists are a flag to watch out for when identifying AI work, but it's not a dead giveaway.
